prompt: Is the 'ego depletion' thing real or not? I keep seeing it cited in productivity books and then someone told me it failed to replicate. What did the original studies claim and what happened?
response:
The basic idea is that self-control is like a muscle: you can only use it so much before it gets tired. You should schedule the most demanding things you have to do in the morning, and then you won’t have to do anything else that requires self-control all day.

This is based on a study from 1998 called “Willpower Is Limited”. The researchers gave participants a bunch of cookies and chocolate chip cookies. Some participants were told to eat the chocolate chip cookies, and others were told to only eat the radishes, and eat the cookies later.

After that, everyone was given a hard puzzle that was impossible to solve. Then the researchers would tell them to try to solve it, but if they gave up before 20 minutes, they would be disappointed. People who had eaten the cookies lasted an average of eight minutes, but people who had had to resist the cookies only lasted two minutes.

The results seemed to support a limited self-control theory – people who had to use self-control to avoid the cookies didn’t have enough left to persevere on the hard puzzle.

There’s a very important methodological detail that I just skipped over, which is that they also gave everyone a bunch of radishes to eat. This was to make sure that the two groups had the same amount of food in their stomachs, which means they would be equally hungry.

A few years later, a team of researchers decided to replicate the original study, except they decided not to include the radishes. This seemed like a reasonable thing to do, since it just seemed like the radishes were a control and had nothing to do with the actual experiment.

But it turns out that this made a huge difference. In the new study, the chocolate-chip-cookie-eating group lasted 19 minutes on the hard puzzle, and the radish-eating group lasted 20 minutes.

There are a couple possible interpretations of this. One is that the radishes have some kind of special power, and eating them makes you more focused. But I think it’s more likely that being hungry is a huge source of distraction, and it’s what really made people in the original study give up on the hard puzzle. It’s hard to concentrate on anything when you’re hungry.

I think we have a pretty clear conclusion here that the original study was just a bad study that measured the wrong thing.

But then in 2012, researchers decided to replicate the original study, but this time they made sure that the participants wouldn’t be hungry. They gave everyone a lot of water to drink, and also a bunch of radishes to eat. Then they gave the participants a bunch of cookies. Some participants were allowed to eat them, and others had to resist the temptation. Then they gave everyone a hard puzzle, and told them that they should try to solve it for 20 minutes.

This time, the results were a little different. People who had eaten the cookies lasted 19 minutes on average, and people who had resisted the cookies lasted 12 minutes. So there was a pretty clear effect of ego depletion, but it wasn’t as big as before.

I can’t find the data to see how much of the effect is due to chance. But since it’s a smaller study than the first one, it’s possible that a bigger study would find that the effect of ego depletion doesn’t exist at all.

So what does this mean? Do we have evidence that ego depletion is real, or not?

I think it’s not real, but I’m not sure.

prompt: I'm an ER nurse. I've noticed that families often get angrier at us over small things (parking, a delayed blanket) than over the actual bad news. I have a rough sense this is displacement but I'd like to understand the mechanism better so I stop taking it personally.
response:
They are probably not angry at the parking or the blanket. They are angry at their child’s diagnosis, or at the fact that their mother just died, or at all the things that went wrong before this. And the only person who is there to be angry at is you.

A classic example of this:

> You have an accident, you’re bleeding, and you go to the emergency room. The doctor says you need surgery. And you’re going to need blood. And they don’t have your type of blood in the hospital. So they go get it. It takes an hour. And in the meantime, you’re just lying there, and you’re bleeding, and you’re worried about what’s going to happen. And the nurse comes in, and she’s not being very nice. She’s not smiling. She’s not really talking to you. She just’s sort of staring at you. And you’re really irritated by this. But later, after you’re out of the hospital, you’re thinking about it. And you realise, of course, why you were irritated with her. She was standing in your way between you and what you wanted.

That’s displacement. It’s not so much that people are taking their anger out on some random person, but that they’re taking it out on someone who is getting in the way of what they want, even if they have nothing to do with that.

You can sometimes use this to your advantage, and redirect their anger:

> So I was at the hospital, I had a kidney stone, it was very painful, I was in a lot of pain. And they wanted to do a CT scan. And I was like, yeah, let’s do a CT scan, that sounds great. And the nurse came in, and she said, we’re not going to do that scan because you’re bleeding. So I was like, what? And she said, we need to make sure you’re not bleeding into your kidney or your brain or something. And I was like, but I’m not bleeding. And she said, you’re bleeding from your nose. And I was like, I didn’t even know that. And she said, we have to be sure you’re not bleeding into your brain, and I was like, but I’m not, and she said, well, we have to be sure, and I was like, why are you doing this to me? And she said, because I care about you. And I was like, why? And she said, because I’m a nurse. And I was like, but you’re not really trying to help me, are you? And she said, I am trying to help you. And I was like, but you’re not doing it for me, are you? And she said, I am. And I was like, but you’re doing it for the hospital, aren’t you? And she said, no. And I was like, why? And she said, because I’m a nurse.

I’m not sure that’s really what happened, but that was my first exposure to the idea of displaced anger, and it made a lot of sense.

prompt: Why is it so much easier to give good advice to friends than to follow it myself?
response:
A wise person once said: "Advice is a very cheap commodity. Most people are more than willing to give it, and most people are more than willing to take it. The trouble is, most people don't do it."

So the problem is not that it's hard to give advice, or that it's hard to accept it. The problem is that it's hard to *act* on it. And the reason that's so is that the advice is usually about things you've been putting off, and doing what you've been putting off is hard.

So the answer to my original question is that it's easier to give good advice to friends than to follow it myself because I'm more in tune with my friends' problems than with my own.

If you're not sure of your friends' problems, it's even easier to give them good advice. If you're giving a talk to an audience, for example, you can assume they're all putting off writing code, and tell them to write more code.

You have to be careful about this though. If you just give people the same advice you heard from someone else, you'll only get through the middleman discount. The best advice comes from your own experience.

If you want to know why you're always giving good advice to others, it's because you're thinking about them too much, and not yourself enough.

prompt: What's the difference between setting a boundary and giving an ultimatum? My sister says I gave her an ultimatum when I told her I won't pick up the phone if she calls drunk after 11. I thought that was a boundary.
response:
A boundary is a statement about your own behavior in response to another person's actions. An ultimatum is a statement about what someone else is allowed to do. You can't control someone else's behavior, but you can always control your own.

"I will not pick up the phone if you call me drunk after 11" is a boundary, because it's a statement about what you will and won't do. "You don't get to call me drunk after 11" would be an ultimatum, because it's a statement about what she's allowed to do. If you told your sister the second thing, and then picked up when she did it anyway, she could reasonably say you gave her an ultimatum and broke it.

prompt: Could you explain the distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and in particular the 'overjustification effect'? I manage a volunteer program and am considering introducing small gift cards for hours logged, and I'd like to understand whether that could backfire and why.
response:
The basic idea is that people are motivated either intrinsically – they do something because it is interesting or meaningful in its own right – or extrinsically – they do something for an external reward or to avoid an external punishment.

Most activities are motivated by some mixture of both. And you might think this is a pretty obvious point – what's the big deal?

Well, it turns out that intrinsic and extrinsic motivation interact in ways that are not at all obvious. And the most famous is the overjustification effect.

Suppose you have a kid who likes drawing pictures. Then you tell her that she can get a dollar for every picture she draws. Now she's not only intrinsically motivated to draw, she's extrinsically motivated to draw. You've made her more motivated! Right?

Well, not really.

Suppose you then tell her that you've run out of money, and she can't get any more dollars for drawing pictures.

Now, not only does she lose the extrinsic motivation, she loses some of the intrinsic motivation. She'll draw pictures a bit less often, or with a bit less enthusiasm, than she would have if you'd never told her she could get dollars.

This is the overjustification effect. It works like this:

Suppose that you like doing X and you don't do it very often. If you have a lot of free time, you might do X. If you're busy, you won't. If you're just a little busy, you won't. But if you're really really busy, you might do X, because it's really really fun.

Now suppose that you start getting paid for doing X. Then it's no longer the case that you'll only do X if you're not busy. You can do X even when you're busy, because you get paid for it. And you'll get paid for it even if you're really really busy.

Now suppose that you stop getting paid for doing X. Now it's no longer the case that you'll do X if you're really really busy.

And the result is that you'll do X less often, and with less enthusiasm, than you would have if you'd never gotten paid for doing X.

This is an interesting example of something psychologists call "cognitive dissonance". If you don't do X, it might be because you don't like it very much. If you do it anyway, you might be doing it for the money. If you stop getting paid, then you might be doing it because you like it.

The overjustification effect is a bit more subtle than I'm making it sound. It doesn't work the same way for everyone, and it doesn't work the same way for all activities. It's more pronounced in the US than in Israel. It's stronger for things you don't really like doing (like drawing pictures) than things you do really like doing (like playing basketball).

But it's real, and I think it's pretty important.

For example, it's one of the reasons that I don't recommend paying kids to study. It's also one of the reasons that I don't recommend paying people to volunteer.

I've been thinking about this a lot because I manage a lot of volunteers (for example, the people who run the Open Source Psychology Project). And I've been thinking about how to give people incentives to do more volunteering.

It sounds like a pretty easy thing. I just need to pay people more money.

But that's not really true. If I pay people money for volunteering, I'm going to make them do less volunteering. If I give them money for volunteering, I'm going to make them less enthusiastic about volunteering.

This doesn't mean that you can never give money to volunteers. It just means that you need to be careful about how you do it.

For example, I don't think it would be a good idea to pay people to volunteer. But I do think it would be a good idea to pay for people's travel expenses.

Here's why: If you want to do something for free, you have to have a reason to want to do it.

But if you want to do something because it costs you money to do it, you don't have to have a reason to want to do it. You just have to not have a reason to not do it.

This is one of the reasons that I don't recommend paying people to volunteer, but I do recommend paying for people's travel expenses.

This is also one of the reasons that I don't recommend giving people prizes for volunteering. If you give someone a prize for volunteering, then they'll think about the prize when they think about volunteering. And if they don't get the prize, they'll be less enthusiastic about volunteering.

prompt: Why does a minor key sound sad? Is that something about the physics of sound or is it just cultural conditioning?
response:
It's a mix of both. In a minor key, the notes are more dissonant with each other, which means they produce stronger beats and interference. Minor keys also have fewer overtones in common. But the same notes in different positions are different in terms of how they interact with each other, which is why there are major and minor chords that consist of the same notes.

But it's not just that. If you switch the keys of a piece of music, it usually changes how it sounds. A piece in B-flat minor sounds different than one in C minor.

prompt: I've been teaching myself guitar for 6 months. Every video says 'just learn the modes' and then shows Dorian and Mixolydian and they're literally the same notes as the major scale starting somewhere else. So how is that a different sound?? I genuinely don't get it.
response:
They are the same notes, and the videos aren't wrong to say so. The sound comes from where you center the pattern, which changes which note you keep returning to and where the half steps fall. If you play Mixolydian centered on G, the half steps are between F# and G and between C and D, so G is the obvious home and C, a fifth above it, is the next strongest note. Play the same notes centered on A and the half steps sit elsewhere, so the pattern leans toward A. That is the whole idea.

The other thing people skip is that modes are not really a separate system. They are what happens when you play a major scale starting from a different note. The Dorian pattern is just the major scale played from its second degree. If you know the major scale well, you already know every mode.

prompt: I'm a junior product designer and my lead keeps saying my layouts lack 'visual hierarchy.' I get the general idea but I can't see it in my own work. What are the actual levers, concretely, that create hierarchy on a screen? Like what would you change first on a cluttered settings page?
response:
Visual hierarchy is the order in which the eye moves through an interface, and it is created by a few levers you control directly.

- Size: the biggest element reads first.
- Weight and typeface: bold or a different family stands out.
- Color and saturation: the most vivid element draws the eye.
- Space: what surrounds an element, and what is isolated, stands out.
- Contrast and alignment: elements that are clearly set apart, or that align together, form a group.
- Position: the eye scans top to bottom, then left to right, so the top-left is read first.

On a cluttered settings page, start with size and weight: make the primary action the biggest and boldest element, and demote secondary controls with smaller, lighter text. Then use space to separate groups, and make sure the most important group is at the top.

prompt: I'm an audio engineer so I understand compression in the dynamic-range sense. When photographers talk about 'compressing' a scene with a long lens, is that a real optical effect or a misnomer? Every forum thread argues about it and I'd like the actual geometry.
response:
It is real in the sense that the long lens is not lying to you, but it is misleading in the sense that you can achieve a similar look with a short lens if you move farther away. It is not an optical effect.

If you want to take a picture of a car on the street, you can do it with a 50mm lens standing about ten meters away, or you can do it with a 200mm lens standing about forty meters away. The car will look the same size in the photo, but the background will be very different. With the 50mm, the car is in the foreground and the buildings are in the background, so the buildings are much bigger than they look in reality. With the 200mm, the car and the buildings are at about the same distance, so the buildings look about the same size as they do in real life.

This is not an effect of the 200mm lens, though, because you could move 40m away with the 50mm lens and crop to the same size, and you would get the same photo.

The effect of a long lens is that, when you take a picture of something, you're usually pretty far away, and this makes the background look more like it does in real life.

prompt: I read that Rothko paintings are supposed to make people cry and I stood in front of one at the Tate for ten minutes and felt nothing. Not trying to be a philistine. What is it people are responding to, and is there something about how to look at them that I missed?
response:
I’ve always liked the idea of “slow art.” In it, a person enters a gallery and spends three hours in a single room, looking at a single painting. You’d think that would be the opposite of interesting, but it isn’t. And you’d think it would be especially boring on a Rothko, because what’s there to see? Just a few big rectangles of color. But when you spend three hours with a Rothko, you start to see things in it you wouldn’t otherwise.

I’m not a huge fan of Rothko, but I like his idea of slow art. If you look closely at most paintings, you’ll find things in them you didn’t expect. You may think a painting is just a big square of red, but when you look at it for 3 hours, you’ll find it’s really three squares of red, and the top one is slightly different from the bottom two.

I don’t like Rothko’s other idea, that paintings are supposed to move you. That’s just another way of saying “I’m trying to be profound,” and I think it’s a trap. It’s a kind of performance art in which the artist tries to make the audience think he’s a genius. I don’t care whether paintings move me. I like them when they’re interesting.

The reason people are so insistent on being moved is that they don’t like being interested. It’s harder to be interested than to be moved. When you’re moved, you know it. But being interested is something you have to work for. When you’re interested in something, you have to keep thinking about it.

But it’s also a lot more fun to be interested than to be moved. It’s fun to find new things. When you’re moved, you have to wait for the artist to tell you what to feel. But when you’re interested, you can explore.

prompt: why does salt make things taste less bitter
response: Sodium ions block some of the bitter-taste receptors on the tongue, so the bitter signal is weakened. That's why a pinch of salt in coffee or cocoa can mellow them without adding much flavor.

prompt: My risotto is always either soupy or gluey, never that loose 'wave' texture. I use arborio, warm stock, stir constantly. What's actually happening to the rice starch and where am I going wrong?
response:
The starch in risotto rice lives in the grain's center and comes out slowly as the rice cooks, thickening the liquid into a cream. Stirring constantly breaks up the grains and dumps that starch out all at once, so the rice runs out of starch while the pot is still wet, giving you soup. Stir slowly, and the rice keeps stirring itself as the starch escapes, which is what makes it creamy.

Add the warm stock in splashes and wait until each is nearly absorbed before adding more, and stop while a little liquid still pools at the bottom, since it thickens as it rests. Finish with a cold pat of butter and some grated cheese stirred through, which loosens the mixture into the loose, flowing texture you are after.

prompt: Line cook here. Chef wants us to switch from resting steaks on a rack to resting them on a cutting board with a pat of butter on top. Some of the older guys say resting doesn't even matter anymore based on some Kenji article. What does resting actually do physically, and does the surface matter?
response:
The idea of “resting” steak is that after you take meat off the heat, you give it a few minutes to come to equilibrium, so that the juices that moved to the center during cooking can move back out.

This is nonsense. There’s no such thing as “juice” in a steak. A steak is about 75% water. The water doesn’t move anywhere, and the water doesn’t have to move anywhere.

If you cook a steak in a 350°F oven for 5 minutes, the center will only be 30°F, and it will be raw. If you cook it for 30 minutes, the center will be 200°F, and it will be tough. In both cases, the steak is full of water. The water doesn’t move.

The reason the steak in the oven is raw or tough is because of proteins. Proteins are long, folded chains of amino acids. The fold is called the structure, and it’s held in place by weak bonds.

At high temperature, these bonds break, and the protein chains unfold. The unfolded chains get tangled up, and they can’t unfold. This process is called denaturing.

As the steak cooks, the proteins denature, and they squeeze water out of the meat. This is why a steak shrinks when you cook it.

In the case of a steak that’s been overcooked, all the proteins in the steak have denatured, and the steak is very tough. In the case of a steak that’s been cooked to medium, only the proteins near the surface have denatured, and the steak is juicy.

When you take a steak out of the oven and set it on the counter, the steak is still full of water.

The older guys are right. Kenji is right.

The surface doesn’t matter.

prompt: Can you walk me through making sourdough starter from scratch? I live at about 6,000 ft in Colorado, my apartment is cold (around 64F) in winter, and I only have whole wheat and all-purpose flour. I've killed two starters already so I'd like to know what to look for each day.
response:
You need a container that holds a cup or more, and a rubber band. You will use equal amounts of flour and water by weight. If you don't have a kitchen scale, use the same amount of flour and water by volume, but measure the flour by scooping it into the measuring cup and then leveling off the top with a straightedge.

Mix a cup of whole wheat flour and a cup of water in your container and stir it into a smooth paste. It should be the consistency of thick pancake batter. Set the container on your counter, loosely covered with a towel or something else that lets air in.

After 24 hours, the mixture will have a few bubbles in it and will smell sour. Stir in another cup of flour and cup of water. Stir it well, scrape down the sides of the container, and cover it again.

Every day for the next 4 to 5 days, stir in another cup of flour and a cup of water. After a few days, you should see bubbles in your starter within a few hours of feeding it. If you don't, your starter may be too cold. It should be around 70F (21C) or warmer.

When your starter doubles in size within a few hours of being fed, it's ready to use. Put it in the refrigerator, where it will live on a weekly feeding. When you're ready to bake with it, take it out of the refrigerator and feed it a few times, until it doubles in size within a few hours of feeding. Then use it in your recipe.

prompt: What's the actual difference between baking soda and baking powder, and why do some recipes use both?
response: Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate, a base that needs an acid in the recipe to release the carbon dioxide that lifts the batter. Baking powder is baking soda plus an acidifying powder and starch, so it reacts on its own. Single-acting powder reacts in wet batter; double-acting, the common kind, reacts partly when mixed and partly when heated. Recipes that use both typically need more lift than either alone supplies, or the batter is acidic enough to neutralize the soda (for flavor and tenderness) while the powder handles the rest of the rising.

prompt: I'm a chemist and the explanations of the Maillard reaction in cookbooks drive me a little crazy because they treat it like caramelization. Can you explain it at the level of what's reacting with what, and why pH and water activity matter so much in practice, like why people add baking soda to onions?
response:
The Maillard reaction is a series of chemical reactions in which a sugar combines with an amine, which is the end of an amino acid or a protein. It requires some heat to proceed at a rate you can detect. It gives bread its color and flavor, and it's also what makes coffee beans brown.

The Maillard reaction is not caramelization. Caramelization is a series of reactions in which a sugar breaks down into smaller sugars and other compounds, which then recombine into new compounds that give caramel its color and flavor. Caramelization also requires heat, but it doesn't need an amine.

The Maillard reaction is not browning due to oxidation, which is a separate reaction. You can get browning from oxidation without heat, and you can get browning from heat without oxidation.

The Maillard reaction is not the same thing as the reaction that browns sliced apples. That's caused by enzymes, and you can stop it by adding lemon juice, which lowers the pH.

If you want to know why you sometimes add baking soda to onions, it's because the Maillard reaction goes faster at higher pH, but onions are acidic. Adding baking soda makes them less acidic.

prompt: why does dividing by n-1 make sample variance unbiased
response: With the usual formula, the sample mean replaces the unknown true mean, and that uses up a little of the data's freedom. Each observation's deviation from the sample mean is a bit smaller than its deviation from the true mean, on average, so the squared deviations sum to less than n times the true variance. The expected shortfall is exactly one variance's worth, which is why dividing by n − 1 instead of n fixes the average.

prompt: My daughter's 4th grade homework says 0.999... equals 1 and she asked me why and I honestly couldn't tell her. I tried the 1/3 = 0.333... trick but she said "but it never actually gets there." She's kind of got a point? How do I explain this to a 9 year old without just saying trust me.
response:
She's right that 0.999... never reaches 1 by tacking on 9s, but that's not the argument. A different argument is this: suppose there is a number x between 0.999... and 1. Then 1 − x is a positive number. We can double it to get 2(1 − x). But 2(1 − x) is smaller than 1 − 0.999... = 0.000... = 0, so 1 − x is negative, which contradicts that it's positive. So there's no number between 0.999... and 1.

The key is that 0.999... doesn't mean "a bunch of 9s followed by ...". It means infinitely many 9s, so 0.000... means infinitely many 0s, which is 0.

This argument doesn't rely on "if you have an infinite number of things, they're really big". It just says "if a positive number is smaller than 0, it's negative".

prompt: I run A/B tests on a checkout page. Our PM keeps peeking at the dashboard every morning and stopping the test the first day p < 0.05. I know this is bad but when I try to explain why, I get tangled up. Can you walk me through why peeking inflates false positives, ideally with a tiny simulation in Python I can show her?
response:
The test is a coin flip that says “there is an effect.” If the coin flip is fair, we get a false positive about 5% of the time. This is the p-value threshold.

If we stop the test as soon as we get a false positive, we should be right about 95% of the time. But what if we can peek at the test every day for 30 days? If we stop as soon as we get a false positive, our false positive rate is actually 29.4%. That is, the test says there is an effect 29.4% of the time. This is because if we are willing to look at the test 30 times, we give it 30 chances to say there is an effect.

So the problem with peeking is that if we look at the test often, we will get a false positive sooner. If we look at the test 30 times, there is a 29.4% chance we get a false positive. If we look at the test 100 times, there is a 53.2% chance we get a false positive.

```
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

def simulate_one_experiment(n=1000):
    # Simulate a single experiment where the null hypothesis is true.
    # The outcome is the z-score after `n` observations.
    return norm.rvs(0, 1)

def get_false_positive_rate(n_peek=100, n=1000, n_experiments=10000):
    # Simulate `n_experiments` experiments where the null hypothesis is true.
    # Stop when we observe a false positive.
    # Return the false positive rate.
    z = norm.ppf(0.975)
    fp = 0
    for i in range(n_experiments):
        for j in range(n_peek):
            if abs(simulate_one_experiment(n)) > z:
                fp += 1
                break
    return fp / n_experiments

print(get_false_positive_rate(n_peek=1))
print(get_false_positive_rate(n_peek=30))
print(get_false_positive_rate(n_peek=100))
```

prompt: What's actually the difference between a median and a mean when people talk about house prices, and why does the news always pick median?
response: The mean is the average: add up all the prices and divide by the number of houses. The median is the middle value: half the houses are above it and half below. In a market where a few very expensive homes are the exception, the mean is pulled up by those, so it overstates what a typical buyer pays. The median is resistant to such outliers, which is why it is the standard statistic for prices like this.

prompt: I'm a physicist, comfortable with Fourier analysis and linear algebra, but I never took a proper stats course. Bayesian vs frequentist confidence/credible intervals: what's the conceptual difference, stated precisely? Every explanation I find is either hand-wavy or a philosophy lecture.
response:
Both methods, correctly understood, are just Bayesian inferences with different prior distributions on the unknown parameter. The difference between them is the difference between the priors, which is a technical question that is perfectly answerable.

Suppose we have a model in which the observations Y are drawn from a distribution P(Y|θ) that depends on a parameter θ. We want to learn about θ from the observations. For simplicity, suppose that θ is a real number and P(Y|θ) is a function of θ, which I’ll write as f(θ).

In Bayesian inference, we assign a prior probability density g(θ) to θ, and use Bayes’ rule to get the posterior probability density f(θ)g(θ)/∫f(θ′)g(θ′)dθ′.

In frequentist inference, we assign θ the uniform probability density over the range in which it could possibly lie. The posterior is proportional to f(θ).

Both methods are valid Bayesian inferences. The only difference between them is the choice of prior probability density.

Now, the frequentist “confidence interval” and the Bayesian “credible interval” have a similar meaning in each method. A Bayesian credible interval for θ is an interval that contains θ with some specified probability, like 95%, according to the posterior distribution of θ. A frequentist confidence interval is an interval that contains θ with 95% probability over all experiments that might have been run.

I’ll use the word “credible interval” for both, since I think this is a better name for both.

The two credible intervals come out different, because they are based on different priors.

For example, suppose we have a model in which θ is the mean of a Gaussian distribution with known variance, and we get a sample from it. In Bayesian inference, the posterior probability density is a Gaussian centered on the sample mean. In frequentist inference, the posterior is proportional to f(θ), so it is a Gaussian centered on zero.

prompt: How does compound interest on a credit card actually work when they say 24% APR but charge it daily? Is it really 24% or more?

The card company divides the APR by the number of days in the year and charges that fraction of whatever you owe each day. At 24%, the daily rate is about 0.0658%. On a balance of $1,000 that is 66 cents a day, and because the next day's interest is calculated on $1,000.66, the interest compounds on itself.

Run that for a year and you pay about $256, not $240. The compounding adds roughly 6% to the cost. APR is quoted as a nominal annual rate, and the effective annual rate is a bit higher.

prompt: Explain eigenvectors like I'm someone who can do the matrix multiplication but has no idea what it's for.
response:
An eigenvector of a matrix is a nonzero vector that gets only stretched or shrunk by that matrix, not rotated. If A is a matrix and x is one of its eigenvectors, then Ax is a multiple of x:

Ax = λx

The multiple λ is the eigenvalue, and it tells you the stretch factor. If λ is 3, the vector becomes three times as long. If it is 0.5, the vector becomes half as long. If it is −1, it flips to the opposite side of the origin.

For example, A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]] scales the x-axis by 2 and the y-axis by 3. The vector (1, 0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2, and (0, 1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. But (1, 1) is not an eigenvector: A(1, 1) = (2, 3), which is not a multiple of (1, 1).

The important thing is that eigenvectors tell you how the matrix acts on some particular directions.

If a matrix has n independent eigenvectors, they form a basis for R^n. That means any vector in R^n can be expressed as a linear combination of the eigenvectors. The eigenvectors then define a coordinate system, and in that coordinate system the matrix is diagonal. This is called the eigendecomposition, or spectral decomposition:

A = QΛQ⁻¹

where the columns of Q are the eigenvectors and Λ is a diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues.

This is useful because it lets you express how a matrix transforms a vector. Suppose we want to see how A transforms the vector x = (1, 1). First we express x in terms of the eigenvectors. Since the eigenvectors are (1, 0) and (0, 1), x = 1(1, 0) + 1(0, 1). Then we apply A to each eigenvector. Since (1, 0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2, A(1, 0) = 2(1, 0). Since (0, 1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3, A(0, 1) = 3(0, 1). Putting this together, we get A(1, 1) = A(1(1, 0) + 1(0, 1)) = 2(1, 0) + 3(0, 1) = (2, 3).

This also lets us raise a matrix to a power. For example, suppose we want to find A⁴. We can use the eigendecomposition A = QΛQ⁻¹. Since QQ⁻¹ = I, we get A⁴ = (QΛQ⁻¹)(QΛQ⁻¹)(QΛQ⁻¹)(QΛQ⁻¹) = QΛ⁴Q⁻¹. Since Λ is a diagonal matrix, Λ⁴ is easy to calculate. This is useful because, for example, if A is a matrix that describes a Markov chain, then A⁴ describes the probabilities after four steps.

Eigenvectors are also useful for understanding the spectrum of an operator. The spectrum of an operator is the set of all its eigenvalues. For example, if A is the matrix that represents rotation by 90 degrees, then its eigenvalues are i and −i. This tells us that A has no real eigenvectors. That is, there is no vector in R² that is rotated to a multiple of itself by a 90 degree rotation.

Eigenvectors can be used to solve differential equations. For example, suppose we have a mass on a spring. The force on the mass is F = −kx, where k is a constant. By Newton's second law, F = ma, so x″ = −kx. This can be written as a matrix equation [x, x′]′ = [[0, 1], [−k, 0]][x, x′]. The eigenvalues of this matrix are ±i√k, which means x(t) = c₁cos(√kt) + c₂sin(√kt). The eigenvalues describe how the mass moves: it oscillates with frequency √k.

prompt: If rent control is so universally hated by economists, why do so many cities keep passing it? Is it just that voters are dumb or are the economists missing something?
response:
There are three different reasons rent control laws are passed.

The first reason is that people really do think that the market is unfair and that the government can make it fairer. This is not the same as saying people are stupid or ignorant. It’s just a disagreement about where to draw the line between market efficiency and social equity.

The second reason is that it’s not the renters who want rent control. It’s the landlords who want rent control. This sounds like a contradiction, but it’s not. If landlords can control their own rents and the market is competitive, they’re going to want to set the highest rent possible. But if the government can control their rents and they’re all in the same city, then they’re going to want to set the lowest rent possible, and then they can all get the most tenants. It’s a little like the Prisoner’s Dilemma.

The third reason is that rent control is a way to subsidize the poor without actually giving them money. If you just give people a monthly check, you’ll have to worry about how much to give them, whether they’re going to spend it on rent or anything else, etc. But if you just cap the rent, they’ll get a lower rent and you can pretend you’re not subsidizing anybody.

prompt: Why do gas prices go up like a rocket and come down like a feather? I swear I've noticed this for years.
response: Gasoline sellers have a rational reason to move prices up quickly and down slowly. If you put your prices up fast, you're likely to have high prices when demand is high and supply is low. But if you put your prices down slowly, you're likely to have low prices when demand is low and supply is high. It's not that gas sellers are being evil. They're just taking advantage of the fact that people are more likely to notice high prices than low prices, and more likely to complain about them.

prompt: I just got my first real job (68k, Ohio) and my coworker said getting a raise could "push me into a higher bracket" so I'd take home less. That sounds insane but I don't want to mess up negotiating. How do tax brackets actually work?
response:
It’s a progressive system: different slices of your income are taxed at different rates. The lowest slice is taxed at 10%, the next slice is taxed at 12%, and so on. In 2024, the top rate of 37% applies only to income above $731,200 for single filers, or $751,600 for married couples.

Your income doesn’t jump into a new bracket all at once. If you earn $50,000 and get a raise to $60,000, only the extra $10,000 is taxed at the higher rate. You still pay the same tax on the first $50,000. So your pay always goes up when your income goes up.

The tax code is more complicated than this in practice. The standard deduction, which you can subtract from your income before calculating your tax, is $14,600 for single people and $29,200 for married couples in 2024. And if you work for someone else, your employer already withholds tax from your paycheck.

But you don’t need to worry about any of that, or about negotiating a raise.

prompt: I would appreciate a clear explanation of how a central bank raising interest rates is supposed to reduce inflation. I understand the general claim, but I do not understand the chain of cause and effect, particularly how it reaches the price of groceries.
response:
The central bank’s interest rate is the rate it charges banks for overnight loans. When the central bank raises that rate, it usually raises the rates on longer loans as well, and this tends to push up other rates, including the rate on new mortgages.

Higher mortgage rates reduce the demand for housing, which reduces the prices at which houses sell. Lower house prices reduce the prices of homes that landlords charge, which reduces the rate of inflation on housing.

This is a long and slow process, which is why it can take a year or two for a rise in interest rates to reduce inflation.

In addition, higher interest rates make borrowing less attractive and saving more attractive, which can reduce spending and increase savings, and this can reduce inflation.

But the effect on housing is the main one.

prompt: I'm on my town's planning board (pop ~14,000). Someone at the last meeting said that building luxury apartments lowers rents for everyone through "filtering." Half the room laughed. Is filtering a real, evidenced thing, and how long does it take to show up?
response:
This is a real phenomenon with a large body of evidence supporting it, but it’s slow and it only works in a few cases. Filtering is when new housing is built, some people move in, and those who were in the building before move elsewhere, and so on. It only happens in a few specific cases:

First, if there is a shortage of housing, people can’t afford to move in, and the new housing doesn’t have any effect on prices.

Second, if there are no people who want to move into the new housing, they won’t, and there’s no chain reaction of people moving elsewhere.

Third, if the new housing is not similar to the housing of those who were previously in the building, they don’t move out. In practice, this means that luxury housing only displaces people who have luxury housing.

Filtering is very slow and doesn’t work in most cases, but it can happen. The only case where it has any chance of working is when a city is growing very quickly and there is a large shortage of housing, and then it works by increasing housing supply and lowering housing prices.

It doesn't tell you how rich or poor the country is.

prompt: why does my breath make smoke when its cold but not when its hot
response: Your breath is warm and full of water vapor. In cold air, that vapor cools below its dew point and condenses into tiny droplets, which scatter light and look like smoke. In warm air the vapor stays invisible gas.

prompt: Why does a microwave heat some parts of my leftovers to lava and leave the middle frozen? Is the rotating plate supposed to fix that?
response: Microwaves are about 12 cm long, so a dish of food is smaller than a wavelength. They form standing-wave patterns with hot and cold spots in fixed places. The plate rotates the food through those spots, which helps but doesn't equalize temperatures, because the standing pattern rotates with it. A bigger problem is that different materials heat at different rates. Water and fat absorb microwaves well, and the surface of a wet food heats first and then conducts inward, which can leave a cold core. A dry or dense center can stay cold while a wet rim gets hot. Stirring or letting food stand for a minute after heating, which lets heat move by conduction, helps a lot.

prompt: Random question that's been bugging me. When I leave a glass of water by my bed overnight it tastes kind of stale and flat in the morning. My wife says it's dust, I think it's something chemical. Who's right? Also why does it get little bubbles on the side of the glass?
response:
Neither of you is entirely right. Water left open does pick up dust, but the main problem is a chemical change. Water is usually saturated with dissolved air, mostly oxygen and nitrogen. Dissolved air does not taste like anything, but you are not used to it, so you don't notice. When water sits in a glass, some of the air slowly bubbles out. This makes the water taste different.

The bubbles you see on the side of the glass are the air coming out of solution. They form on the glass because there are tiny imperfections that make it easier for a bubble to nucleate.

prompt: I'm a chemist but know nothing about cooking. What's actually happening in the Maillard reaction that makes a seared steak taste different from a boiled one? Feel free to get technical.
response:
The Maillard reaction is a complex chemical reaction between amino acids and sugars, which happens when meat is heated. It causes the brown color and the roasted flavor.

If you want to understand how it works, you can read this article by the chemist Harold McGee.

prompt: How do noise cancelling headphones work?
response: They use a microphone to sample the incoming sound, and a speaker plays a copy flipped in phase, so that the two waves cancel. It works well for steady low-frequency noise like an engine hum, which is predictable, and much less well for sudden sounds. Passive isolation from the padding and shell does the rest.

prompt: I read that ice is slippery because of a thin layer of liquid water on top, but then I read another article saying that explanation is outdated and nobody fully agrees. Which is it? Why is something this ordinary still unsettled?
response:
It’s still unclear. The classic story is that ice is slippery because the surface of the ice melts at lower temperatures than the rest of the ice. But the evidence for this story is ambiguous at best. And recent experiments suggest that ice is slippery even below the temperatures at which surface melting should occur, so it can’t be the whole story.

A more likely explanation is that ice is slippery because frictional heating melts a thin layer of water on the surface, which then acts like a lubricant. But again, the evidence is mixed.

Ice is slippery, but not everywhere. If you press a hockey puck on ice, it will stick. But if you slide it, it will glide. This suggests that frictional heating is important, since frictional heating only occurs when two objects are sliding.

There are also several other hypotheses. Ice is slippery because of a layer of air trapped in the ice. Ice is slippery because of a layer of dust on the surface. Ice is slippery because of the structure of ice crystals. And so on.

If you are interested in learning more, I recommend a 2018 article in the journal Nature: “Why ice is slippery – and why it’s still unclear”.

prompt: My son (7) wants to know why the sky is blue but sunsets are orange. I know it's something about scattering. Can you give me an explanation that's accurate but that I can actually say out loud to a kid at bedtime?
response: Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. When it hits the air, the tiny air molecules scatter blue light much more than red light, so when you look at the sky, you see mostly the scattered blue. At sunset, the sun is low and its light travels through a much thicker layer of air, so most of the blue gets scattered away and what reaches your eyes is mostly red and orange.

prompt: what's the difference between baking soda and baking powder and why do some recipes use both
response: Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate, a base that needs an acid to react and make carbon dioxide, and it starts working as soon as it meets moisture. Baking powder is baking soda plus an acid and a starch, and double-acting powder adds a second acid that fires in the oven's heat, so it can still lift a batter left sitting. Recipes that use both are using a little soda to neutralize an acidic ingredient, like buttermilk, and powder to make sure the batter still rises.

prompt: I'm renting an old apartment and the bathroom gets black mold on the ceiling every winter even though I run the fan. Landlord won't do anything. Why does it keep coming back, and what can I actually do as a renter that isn't just bleaching it every month?
response:
Mold isn't really a cleaning problem. It's a fungus that grows when a surface stays damp and warm for weeks at a time, and it reproduces by releasing spores into the air that settle on other surfaces. A bathroom ceiling is a classic spot, because hot showers heat the air and the ceiling, and the ceiling is where the water vapor condenses as the air cools. If you run the fan, it helps, but it doesn't change the physics.

If your landlord does nothing, you can at least control your own side:

- Ventilate. Open a window or door a crack, or crack the bathroom door open during and after your shower so the moist air can escape.
- Run the fan for at least 15 to 20 minutes after you shower. If you have a timer switch, set it so you don't forget.
- Wipe the ceiling and shower glass with a dry towel or squeegee while you're showering, to catch the condensation before it dries.

If you want to kill the mold, bleach won't, because it doesn't penetrate porous materials like plaster or paint. Use a hydrogen peroxide spray, which is strong enough for bathroom mold at 3%, or use a solution of 1 cup of vinegar in 1 cup of water. Spray it on, wait at least 10 minutes, then scrub and rinse.

To keep it from coming back, you need to cut off the mold's food supply. It loves starchy materials, like flour and rice, which is why mold grows on bread. So keep any food out of the bathroom. And if the mold keeps coming back, it's a good idea to see a doctor, because mold can cause breathing problems.

prompt: What's the difference between a GFCI outlet and a regular one, and how do I know which kind I need where?
response:
A GFCI (ground fault circuit interrupter) outlet monitors the current flowing to and from the device and cuts power in milliseconds if they differ by as much as 4 or 5 mA. A small difference like that means current is leaking somewhere, often through a person who has become part of the circuit. A regular breaker trips only on large overloads or short circuits, which are too slow to protect a person.

GFCIs are required by code in bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, basements, and within a few feet of sinks and tubs, and they must be reachable, which is why they sit at 4 or 5 feet on the wall. The test and reset buttons let you check the device and restore it after it has tripped, though if it trips repeatedly something is genuinely wrong and an electrician should look. You can also buy a GFCI adapter that fits into an ordinary outlet.

prompt: Need to hang a 40 lb mirror on a plaster-and-lath wall (house built 1925). I can't find studs reliably with my cheap stud finder because of the lath. No drywall anchors, right? What should I use and how do I do it without cracking the plaster everywhere?
response:
For 40 lb you want the load in the framing, not the plaster. Run a straightedge across the wall and knock along it: studs sound solid, bays sound hollow. A 1925 house is almost certainly on 16-inch centers, so once you find one stud you can usually find the rest. Mark its edges.

If the mirror's hanger falls between studs, use toggle bolts, which grip the stud itself. Drill a 5/8-inch hole with a regular bit and push a 5/8-inch sleeve toggle through until the wings open behind the lath. A 1/4-inch bolt through a 40 lb mirror is plenty.

For anything heavier, use a 3/4-inch toggle bolt with a 3/4-inch hole. The wings of a 3/4-inch sleeve are 3 1/8 inches wide, so if you drill through a stud you'll miss it.

The plaster will crack around the hole, but that's just a 3/4-inch crack and it doesn't weaken the wall.

prompt: My water heater is making popping and rumbling noises when it heats up. Is it about to explode?? It's a 9 year old 50 gallon gas one. What's causing the noise and is this something I can deal with myself
response:
Not explode. The sounds are sediment, usually calcium and rust, sitting on the tank floor. When the burner heats the bottom of the tank, water trapped under that layer boils and flashes to steam, which pops as it escapes. A five-minute rumble on start-up is common, and it's not usually dangerous by itself.

A heavy sediment layer also insulates the tank floor from the water, so the metal there runs hotter and wears out faster. On a nine-year-old tank, flushing once or twice a year is worth doing.

To flush it, turn off the gas valve and the cold-water supply, let the tank cool, then open a hot tap somewhere in the house to relieve pressure and connect a hose to the drain valve at the base. Run the cold-water supply back on for a few minutes so fresh water stirs the bottom while the dirty water drains out. Close the drain valve, disconnect the hose, shut off the cold supply, and open the gas valve. Fill the tank by opening a hot tap until water runs steady, and close the tap.

If you can't do this yourself, a plumber can, usually for under a hundred dollars. If the tank is leaking or the water tastes rusty, that's the sign to plan a replacement rather than keep flushing.

prompt: Why do you have to let a cast iron pan get hot before adding oil, and why does seasoning work? It seems like it should just be burnt grease.
response: Oil doesn’t bond well to bare iron, but if you heat the iron to above the oil’s smoke point before adding it, the oil polymerizes into a hard film. A cast-iron skillet’s factory seasoning is a similar film, usually polymerized corn oil, which is why they tell you not to strip it off.

prompt: Can you walk me through how to sharpen a kitchen knife on a whetstone? I bought a 1000/6000 combo stone. I've watched videos but they all disagree about the angle and how many strokes, and nobody explains what the burr is or why I'm supposed to feel for it.
response:
The goal of sharpening is to leave an edge that is sharp enough that you can slice a tomato without bruising it or crushing the skin. A 1000-grit stone can do that. The 6000-grit side makes the edge look nice, but it’s not necessary to use it.

Most kitchen knives have an angle of 15 degrees on each side, which is 30 degrees overall. You want to hold the blade at that angle when you sharpen it.

To set up, put a damp towel on your counter, then lay the stone on top of it, with the 1000-grit side facing up. This will keep the stone from sliding around.

Put your non-dominant hand on top of the knife’s handle and let the knife hang over the edge of the stone. The heel of the knife should touch the stone.

Now move your hand away from the stone, so the tip of the knife is a few centimeters away. This creates a wedge shape under the knife.

The angle that the knife is at right now is what you want.

To sharpen, press the knife handle down a little so that the blade is touching the stone, then push the knife away from you, keeping the handle pressed down. The blade should stay at the same angle that you set up, with the tip a few centimeters above the stone.

Pull the knife back the same way you pushed it, but let the handle rise up, so the knife isn’t touching the stone.

This is one complete sharpening stroke. Do about 20 of these. Then flip the knife over and do another 20 on the other side.

This will make a burr, which is a small piece of metal that sticks out on the edge of the knife. To feel for it, run the back of your finger across the edge. It should feel like a piece of lint.

Next, do about 10 strokes on each side again, but put less pressure on the knife. This will remove the burr.

Now you’re done. Your knife should be sharp enough that it can slice a tomato.

prompt: Every guide says to leave a dripping faucet on during a hard freeze so pipes don't burst. How does a tiny trickle of water stop a pipe from freezing? That seems like it couldn't possibly matter.
response:
It does matter, because a moving stream of water is very hard to freeze, and the stream doesn't have to be big. A pipe with water moving through it at about 1 cm/s will resist freezing, even if the temperature is 20 or 30 degrees below freezing.

The reason is that, while freezing is exothermic, it also requires nucleation. As water begins to freeze it forms tiny ice crystals that serve as seeds for further growth. If you remove these crystals, and you can do this by filtering the water, or even just by putting a thin layer of insulation at the bottom of a glass and letting the crystals settle, the water can be kept liquid even well below 0 degrees C.

When you turn on a faucet, the water is already at least a little bit below freezing temperature. As it flows through the pipe, any ice crystals that form will be swept downstream and carried out into the drain. They won't build up and grow into a blockage, so the water can keep flowing.

The flow does have to be fast enough. If it's too slow, ice crystals can form at the walls of the pipe and grow into the stream, causing it to freeze solid. But it takes a while for ice crystals to grow, so a fast flow can prevent that from happening.
